text: I think that renovating apartments, it's a compromise. In my thesis, it's less about creating the perfect thing, the perfect aesthetic, perfect functionality. More about balancing all of it, and compromising with what's possible. So, we can renovate, of course, a very ugly apartment, ugly kitchen, make it more beautiful, more functional. Change the floor, the lights, maybe the storage, make it more nice. We can make it more open, brighter. We can make it feel less tired, tired feeling, old. Maybe repaint it. But then, it's not as easy and straightforward as we think. It takes a lot of time, a lot of money, a lot of dust. We never feel that it's done really. We always feel we can change something, improve something. And we sacrifice other things. For example, we can't do a nice kitchen and a nice bathroom at the same time. We can only do one of them. We can open up walls and make the space more open, but then maybe it makes the space noisier or less heated. We also lose the attachment to the place. So, you know, the broken floor or the scratched frame of the door, we lose that. It's very sentimental. It's very difficult, actually. And I think that's why the best renovation is not the one that looks like a magazine or a Pinterest picture. But the one where you compromise and you accept that some things need to change, some things are going to stay, some things can be improved. And you accept imperfection in the end. And I think that in a renovation, you negotiate between who you are, who you were, who you want to be, and how you want to live in your space. And if you do it very patiently, very nicely, very honestly, then it can work very well. And then your space will not just be new. It will feel more home.
